questions.enonce_markdown:
The elements of period three of the periodic table are; sodium, magnesium, Aluminium, silicon, Phosphorus, Sulphur, chlorine and Argon.

(i) Sketch a graph to show the variation of Atomic Radius against atomic number for the elements.

(ii) Explain the shape of the graph in (i) above.

(iii) Complete the table below by either giving the structural form or the formula of an oxide.

| Structural form | Formula of oxide |
|---|---|
| Ionic | |
| | $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ |
| | $\mathrm{Cl_2O}$ |

*[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Sketch.** Axes: atomic number $Z$ from 11 (Na) to 18 (Ar) on the horizontal axis; atomic radius (nm) on the vertical axis. The graph is a **falling curve from Na to Cl, steepest between Na and Al and flattening towards Cl, followed by a sharp rise at Ar.** Typical values (approximate, nm):

| Element | Na | Mg | Al | Si | P | S | Cl | Ar |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $Z$ | 11 | 12 | 13 | 14 | 15 | 16 | 17 | 18 |
| Radius / nm | 0.186 | 0.160 | 0.143 | 0.117 | 0.110 | 0.104 | 0.099 | about 0.19 (van der Waals) |

Metallic radii are used for Na, Mg and Al, covalent radii for Si, P, S, Cl, and the van der Waals radius for argon (no covalent bonds are formed). Exact values depend on the data book; the shape is what matters.

**(ii) Explanation.**

- Across the period the **nuclear charge increases** by one proton per element, while the extra electrons enter the **same outer shell (n = 3)**; the shielding by inner electrons stays almost constant.
- The **effective nuclear charge therefore increases**, pulling the outer electrons closer to the nucleus, so the **atomic radius decreases** from Na to Cl.
- **Argon** does not form bonds, so its radius is the (larger) **van der Waals radius** measured between non-bonded atoms; hence the sharp rise at the end of the period.

**(iii) Table.**

| Structural form | Formula of oxide |
|---|---|
| Ionic (giant ionic lattice) | $\mathrm{Na_2O}$ (or $\mathrm{MgO}$) |
| Giant covalent (macromolecular, giant molecular lattice) | $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ |
| Simple molecular (covalent, small discrete molecules) | $\mathrm{Cl_2O}$ |

$\mathrm{Na_2O}$ is built of $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ions; $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ is a three-dimensional network of Si-O covalent bonds; $\mathrm{Cl_2O}$ consists of separate covalent molecules held by weak van der Waals forces.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The complex ions of the elements of the first transition series undergo isomerism.

(i) Define the following;

A) Complex ion:

B) Isomerism:

(ii) Draw structures to show Geometric isomerism in the complex $\mathrm{Co\,(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2}$.

Isomer 1  /  Isomer 2

(iii) Using the spdf notation, write the electronic configuration of the following ions;

${}_{21}\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$ :

${}_{25}\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ :

(iv) Which of the ions in (iii) above is not coloured? Explain. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Definitions.**

A) A **complex ion** is a species made of a **central metal ion** (or atom) to which a number of **ligands** (molecules or ions that each donate a lone pair of electrons) are bound by **dative covalent (co-ordinate) bonds**; the whole species carries an overall charge, e.g. $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^{n+}}$.

B) **Isomerism** is the existence of **two or more compounds (isomers) with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms**, i.e. different structural or spatial formulae, and therefore different properties.

**(ii) Geometric (cis-trans) isomers** of the octahedral complex $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^{n+}}$ (six ligands round the central Co ion, at the corners of an octahedron):

- **Isomer 1, trans:** the two $\mathrm{H_2O}$ ligands are at **opposite corners** (180 degrees apart, e.g. above and below the cobalt), and the four $\mathrm{NH_3}$ lie in the plane between them.
- **Isomer 2, cis:** the two $\mathrm{H_2O}$ ligands are at **adjacent corners** (90 degrees apart), and the four $\mathrm{NH_3}$ occupy the other four corners.

(To draw: put Co in the centre with bonds drawn as plain lines, wedges and dashes to the six ligands; label NH3 and H2O at the positions described.)

**(iii) Electronic configurations.**

${}_{21}\mathrm{Sc}$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^1 4s^2$, so **$\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$: $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6$** (the $4s^2$ and $3d^1$ electrons are lost).

${}_{25}\mathrm{Mn}$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^5 4s^2$, so **$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$: $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^5$** (the $4s$ electrons are lost first).

**(iv)** **$\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$ is not coloured.** Colour in transition-metal ions comes from **d-d electronic transitions**: in a complex the d orbitals are split into two energy levels, and an electron moves from the lower to the higher level by absorbing a frequency of visible light; the remaining light transmitted is the colour seen. $\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$ has an **empty 3d sub-shell (3d$^0$)**, so no d electron is available to be promoted and no visible light is absorbed: its compounds are white or colourless. $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ($3d^5$) has a partly filled d sub-shell and is coloured (very pale pink).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Contact Process for the production of sulphuric acid involves three stages; the production of sulphur dioxide, sulphur trioxide and sulphuric acid. Write balanced equations for the processes involved in each stage.

Stage 1:

Stage 2:

Stage 3: *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Stage 1 - sulphur dioxide:** burning sulphur in dry air (or roasting iron pyrites):

$\mathrm{S} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO_2}$

(or $4\mathrm{FeS_2} + 11\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 8\mathrm{SO_2}$)

**Stage 2 - sulphur trioxide:** $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and excess air over a vanadium(V) oxide ($\mathrm{V_2O_5}$) catalyst at about $450^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 1-2 atm (a reversible, exothermic reaction):

$2\mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3}$

**Stage 3 - sulphuric acid:** the $\mathrm{SO_3}$ is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to give oleum (dissolving it directly in water forms an acid mist), and the oleum is then diluted with water:

$\mathrm{SO_3} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}$

$\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$

(Overall for stage 3: $\mathrm{SO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_4}$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Nitrogen exhibits oxidation states of -3 to +5 in its compounds. Complete the table below;

| Oxidation state of nitrogen | Formula of compound |
|---|---|
| -3 | |
| | $\mathrm{NH_2OH}$ |
| +2 | |
| +5 | |

*[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Oxidation state of nitrogen | Formula of compound |
|---|---|
| -3 | $\mathrm{NH_3}$ (or $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$, e.g. $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$) |
| **-1** | $\mathrm{NH_2OH}$ |
| +2 | $\mathrm{NO}$ |
| +5 | $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ (or $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$, $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$) |

Check for $\mathrm{NH_2OH}$: $x + 2(+1) + (-2) + (+1) = 0$, so $x = -1$. For $\mathrm{NO}$: $x + (-2) = 0$, so $x = +2$. For $\mathrm{HNO_3}$: $(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0$, so $x = +5$.
